Members of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on
items.text:
Nations agree to ‘elaborate’ on rules for AI-run ‘killer robots’ by 2028
Members of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on a possible accord regulating lethal autonomous weapons, known as “killer robots”, in the next two years.
Saturday’s announcement at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) came after nearly 100 nations pushed for swift adoption of legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
Key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats said Russia’s objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off. Talks over the final wording then ran through the night.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the conference, said some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
He said more than 10 years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.
“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results,” he told reporters as the meeting wrapped up.
He said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.
‘Watered down’
Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down”, saying it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.
Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.
“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told the AFP news agency.
Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, said the outcome was disappointing.
“It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules – but the technology is racing ahead,” she told AFP.

NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21- DCP party leader Rigathi Gachagua has admitted that joining President William Ruto’s UDA party instead of maintaining an independent political vehicle was one of the biggest mistakes he made while in government.
Gachagua said the decision weakened his political position and le
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21- DCP party leader Rigathi Gachagua has admitted that joining President William Ruto’s UDA party instead of maintaining an independent political vehicle was one of the biggest mistakes he made while in government.
Gachagua said the decision weakened his political position and left him unable to protect his interests when his relationship with Ruto deteriorated, eventually leading to his removal from office.
Speaking while hosting a delegation from Gatundu North at his Wamunyoro residence, the former Deputy President recalled how he entered into a political agreement with Ruto when the President already had his own party, arguing that he should have maintained a separate political outfit.
“We ran into trouble by going to a wedding in someone else’s vehicle. When we got to the venue, he told us to get down, and we ran into problems,” Gachagua said.
He used the analogy to explain why he believes politicians should have their own parties rather than depend on political vehicles controlled by others.
According to Gachagua, having an independent party with more than 100 MPs would have given him greater bargaining power and made it difficult for Ruto to sideline him.
“If we had a party, with more than 100 members of parliament, this Kasongo would be respecting us,” he said.
Gachagua further claimed that he could still be serving as Deputy President had he maintained his own political party instead of joining UDA.
“Even if I made an agreement with him while he had UDA, if we had our own party, up to today I would still be in office,” he added.
The DCP leader said his new party would give him the political independence he lacked during his time in government, allowing him to negotiate from a position of strength and protect the interests of his supporters.
“Now we have our own vehicle, and that’s how we’ll get there, get into government, and protect our affairs inside,” he declared.
He also outlined his party’s priorities, promising to push for legislation that protects farmers, traders and other economic groups.
Gachagua said the party would focus on better laws covering tea, coffee, milk, avocados, macadamia, businesses and livestock feeds.
He called on supporters to elect more DCP candidates to Parliament, arguing that a strong parliamentary presence would give the party greater influence in government.
“We must have good representatives in Parliament from our party, with a large number of us,” he said.

Was Vladimir Putin 'snubbed' by Xi Jinping? Viral handshake video is AI fake
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
A viral video appearing to show China's Xi Jinping "snubbing" Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit has racked up millions of views, fuelling speculation about tensions between Beijing and Moscow. But the footage is fake. FRANCE 24 traced the original video to an earlier summit, where the two leaders did shake hands. The creator, who runs a satire account, admitted to manipulating the footage using Grok Imagine, an AI tool developed by Elon Musk's xAI, as Vedika Bahl explains.
Just hours after the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, misinformation about the meeting began circulating on social media, including a viral video supposedly showing a diplomatic snub between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.
The footage appears to show the Russian president approaching Xi and extending his hand for a handshake, only for the Chinese leader to turn away, leaving Putin seemingly humiliated in front of the cameras. The video quickly spread across X, with users describing the moment as a "public insult" and "humiliation" for the Russian president. Others suggested it was evidence of growing tensions between Beijing and Moscow.
The incident however, never happened. The viral clip has been manipulated using artificial intelligence, although it uses footage from a previous meeting.
An old video manipulated with AI
The FRANCE 24 Observers conducted a reverse image search of the viral video, and found it was filmed in August 2026 in Kyrgyzstan, during a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). In the authentic footage, Xi and Putin can clearly be seen shaking hands, with no indication of a diplomatic snub.
The viral clip was thus not only manipulated using AI, but also falsely presented as footage from the recent APEC summit. Video from the APEC gathering in Shenzhen also shows Xi and Putin shaking hands.
Creator admits using AI to fake the encounter
FRANCE 24 managed to trace the manipulated footage back to its original creator, whose post has since accumulated more than 10 million views and was flagged as AI-generated content.
The creator also openly acknowledged using artificial intelligence to produce the video, saying it had been made with Grok Imagine, an AI generation tool developed by Elon Musk's company xAI. In exchanges with other users, the creator expressed satisfaction with how realistic the manipulated footage appeared. The account describes itself as satire and regularly publishes provocative content, including AI-manipulated videos of real-world events.

Germany news: Support for Ukraine military aid waning, survey shows
Published November 21, 2026last updated November 21, 2026
What you need to know
- Almost half of people in Germany want the government to reduce or cut support for Ukraine as it fights Russia's invasion, a survey shows
- Many consumers in Germany will be paying more for electricity and gas from next year, partly because of the war in Iran
- US judge rules Germany's agrochemical giant Bayer must pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from US cancer patients
This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:
US court approves Bayer Roundup cancer settlement
A judge in the US state of Missouri has approved a settlement under which Germany-based agrochemical company Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion (€6.6 billion) over the next two decades to resolve lawsuits from cancer sufferers who say they should have been warned that its weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma.
The settlement, which applies nationwide, means both Roundup users who are already ill with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who develop it in future could an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, with factors such as their use of the product, their age at the time of diagnosis and illness severity determining the exact sum.
The decision could be appealed.
For more on this story, head over to our report.
IN DEPTH: The plight of Gen Z in Germany
Young people in Germany, as in many other parts of the world, have been taking to the streets to demonstrate for a fairer, safer world and a greater say in what policies are enacted by politicians.
But despite the fact that many of their complaints are fully justified, with jobs difficult to find despite a high level of study or training, housing that is increasingly unaffordable and a lack of government action against climate change to ensure the world remains habitable, the demonstrations have sometimes been criticized or even labeled as criminal.
DW looks at the problems facing Gen Z and its fears about its future in a world where young people have little say.
Electricity, gas bills to go up for millions
Many consumers who get their gas and electricity under the standard tariff offered by local utility providers will be paying considerably more for electricity and gas next year, according to comparison website Verivox.
Some 3.7 million households are expected to pay more for electricity, with a rise of some 2% expected.
The rise has been cushioned to some extent by coalition's recent agreement to lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level to protect households and businesses.
Gas will become considerably more expensive for some 1.9 million households, with 361 regional utility providers announcing rises of some 14% for December, January and February.
"The wholesale prices for gas and electricity, which have risen sharply since the Iran war began in March 2026, are only now starting to have an effect on prices for consumers," Verivox energy expert Thorsten Storck said.
Almost half of people in Germany want Ukraine aid cut or dropped
Some 49% of people in Germany would like to see Berlin's financial, military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion either reduced or cut completely, a survey has shown.
In all, 25% of respondents in a YouGov survey wanted aid to Ukraine to be dropped, while 24% were in favor of reducing.
Altogether 30% wanted to retain aid at the current level, and 9% felt it should be raised. Eleven percent were undecided on the issue.
The survey was conducted between November 13 and 16 on behalf of the newspaper Welt am Sonntag.
This week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted a meeting of Ukraine's European allies, known as the "Coalition of the Willing", in a bid to maintain a united front as peace talks in Ukraine continue.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn!
You join us as a survey shows that support for Berlin's help to Kyiv amid the Russian invasion is declinin.
And millions of households will see their electricity and gas bills rise considerably next year amid a number of geopolitical pressures.
Read on for more on these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany this weekend.

items.title: 5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
items.summary:
5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You
items.text:
5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch.
" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.
Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life, says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.
"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."
That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health. Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.
Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists, shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.
The problem: You can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Take 15 minutes to come up with a solution
Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.
Instead of reliving the issue, which is unproductive, take 15 minutes to convert the situation into a problem you can solve, Winch says. "What's the best way of handling it? Do I have a conversation with them? And if I want to have a conversation, what's the outcome I'm trying to get to?"
This approach allows you to create a plan for how to address the situation. "You should feel an ease in stress. Now it will be much easier for you to let go," he says.
The problem: You still can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Distract yourself with a game or a memory task
If you can't stop spinning your wheels about work, try distracting yourself for two or three minutes, Winch says. It can help you reset so you can focus on something else.
"You need something that takes up your mental bandwidth so there's not enough left over for rumination," he says.
He shares a few ideas: Play a puzzle or game like Wordle. Name all the state capitals. Think of whom you sat next to in elementary school. Picture all the items on the top shelf of your fridge.
When you're done, instruct yourself to reengage in whatever you're doing, he says. You might tell yourself, "I really want to enjoy this show now," or "I really want to watch my kid [so I can] talk to her after the game."
The problem: You still feel like you're at work when you're home
The fix: Create boundaries between work and home with immersive rituals
Rituals can train your brain to "shift gears from the mindset of being at work to the family gear, the partner gear, the friendship gear," Winch says.
Your ritual should include as many of your senses as possible, he says. Take a warm shower or a hot bath. Listen to music that puts you in the mood for whatever comes next. Shift the lighting — maybe turn off the bright lights you use at your workstation and light a candle.
One of the most effective things you can do is change your clothing, Winch says. "Clothing makes us feel a certain way. That's why power suits make us feel powerful and leisure wear makes us feel relaxed."
If you work from home and are already in your comfy clothes, change into a different set of comfy clothes when your workday is over, Winch says. It should be something "that your brain can distinguish you wear when you finish working."
The more you repeat these rituals, the more your brain knows when it's time to go from work mode to "being more relaxed and open to engaging with what you're doing when you're home," Winch says.
The problem: You feel drained after work
The fix: Do something that energizes you
One of the mistakes people make after work is they err on the side of relaxing because they feel drained, Winch says. But the things we tend to do while resting, like watching screens or doomscrolling, won't recharge us.
"You have to do something that makes you feel energized, and that's a personal thing," Winch says. If you're an athlete, head to the gym. If you're a maker, create something. If you're an extrovert, get a drink with a friend.
It's a "mental battle to force ourselves" to do these things, especially after a long day at work, he says. But "we're going to sleep better that night and have more pep in our step the next day because of that."
The problem: Work feels like your whole life
The fix: Try this thought experiment
It's OK for work to be a part of your identity, but it shouldn't be the only thing that defines you, Winch says.
If you're losing yourself in your job, try this thought exercise, he says. "If your work disappeared tomorrow, what's left? How would you describe yourself? How would you describe what your life is about?" You may find that your worth likely doesn't come from your job title or salary.
And don't forget what it's all for. If you've got the choice between working for a couple of more hours or watching your favorite TV show with your partner, pick the TV show.
"The only reason why I'm working is to be able to have a life in the first place," Winch says. "And if I end up not having one, then what's the point of it all?"

items.summary:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity
items.text:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.
The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.
That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.
"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.
The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.
Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.
"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.
The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.
"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.
In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety
Competition between AI companies is fierce.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit this week.
That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."
OpenAI also plans to go public, and filed preliminary IPO paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, shortly after Anthropic. But Altman said in September the company has delayed those plans.
In an essay the same month, Amodei discussed the need for AI companies to carefully "pace" the development of frontier models.

items.text:
The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
What happened with stock markets this week?
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
What's behind the steep drops?
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
What are the potential financial consequences?
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness.
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
What does it mean for the economy if the AI boom falters?
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

items.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
items.summary:
An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.
Next year
items.text:
An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.
Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.
If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.
There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.
"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.
Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.
So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.
One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.
And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.
Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.
The practical and legal hurdles
Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."
Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.
Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.
States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.
"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."
But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.
"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."
But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.
Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."
Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.
"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."
A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.
Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.
And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multip

Max Verstappen has won the Las Vegas Grand Prix two of its three years but never sat on the pole — until n
items.text:
Verstappen escapes Vegas F1 discipline, takes pole as Antonelli penalised
Max Verstappen escapes discipline in Vegas F1 practice after run-ins and takes pole as Kimi Antonelli hit with penalty.
Max Verstappen has won the Las Vegas Grand Prix two of its three years but never sat on the pole — until now.
He finally made it to the top spot because of a penalty handed to Kimi Antonelli the day before, giving Verstappen a chance after qualifying second behind the Italian on Friday night.
Antonelli, the 20-year-old who is this year’s Formula 1 champion, put together a time of 1:33.893 in the third qualifying session for Saturday night’s race. But he will start sixth because of a five-place penalty after his Mercedes team exceeded its allocation of engines for the season.
Mercedes — which has already clinched the constructors’ championship — had two of the three fastest cars in qualifying, with George Russell .331 seconds behind his teammate. Russell, who won the Las Vegas Strip two years ago, will start second.
“I think on the whole we’ve been very competitive,” Russell said. “But Max this morning we actually had as the fastest.”
Verstappen, a four-time F1 champion who had quite a combative practice session earlier Friday, was .258 seconds behind Antonelli.
This came after he was summoned by the stewards to explain run-ins with Russell and Franco Colapinto, though no discipline was handed down. Verstappen weaved in front of Russell and then the two went side by side.
They were seated at the post-qualifying news conference with Antonelli between them. Both were asked about coming together on the track.
“Nothing happened,” Verstappen said.
“No confusion,” Russell said. “I think it was pretty clear.”
It had been a rocky couple of days for Verstappen. The Dutch champion let his Red Bull team know twice on the radio in Thursday’s practices that he wasn’t happy with how the car was handling.
“Just trying to get my head around it to try to make the best out of it this weekend,” Verstappen said after qualifying. “I think we had a solid qualifying. We executed well. My first lap in (the third qualifying session) was pretty much as good as it can be. I think to be on the front row is very good for us.”
Antonelli, the youngest series champion ever, has the daunting task of trying to become the first driver to win in Las Vegas by starting third or worse. He has started further back just twice this season — but turned a 15th-place spot on the grid into a victory on July 5 in the British Grand Prix. Antonelli also went from 16th to third on June 14 in Barcelona, Spain.
Even though he posted the fastest lap on Friday, Antonelli was far from pleased.
“It was very weird qualifying for me,” Antonelli said. “First of all, I couldn’t get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car. The brake pedal was very long, so I was struggling on the braking. It was so unexpected, and that last lap I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car, but the tow is so big here, I was able to gain from that and put it on board.”
Conditions for the 3.85-mile course (6.2 kilometres) were considerably different from Thursday’s two practices, the first in the rain and the second on the wet surface that remained. The track was dry for Friday’s practice and qualifying sessions.
That better simulated expected dry conditions for Saturday night’s 50-lap race. Drivers also learned more about driving in what is expected to be one of the colder races in F1 history, with a forecast temperature of 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8 degrees Celsius) at race time.
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc — fourth and fifth in the season standings, respectively — surprisingly failed to get out of the second qualifying session. Leclerc cost himself by not properly handling Turn 7 and didn’t get to the chequered flag in time for a final lap to make the time necessary to make the top 10 for the last session.
Leclerc will start 11th on Saturday and Hamilton 12th.

The office was reportedly defaced overnight, with graffiti bearing the words
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – An office belonging to the Linda Mwananchi Movement in Matungu, Kakamega County, has been vandalised ahead of President William Ruto’s visit to the constituency scheduled for Saturday, November 21.
The office was reportedly defaced overnight, with graffiti bearing the words “TWO TERMS” and “TUTAM” written on the premises, in an incident that has drawn condemnation from Bumula MP Wanami Wamboka.
Wamboka, who serves as the Linda Mwananchi Movement’s Secretary for Public Policy, described the incident as political intimidation and said it would not deter the movement from conducting its activities in the area.
In a statement, the legislator said the vandalism happened ahead of the President’s scheduled tour, accusing those responsible of attempting to intimidate supporters of the movement.
“Our Linda Mwananchi Movement (LMM) office in Matungu was overnight defaced ahead of Mr President’s scheduled tour of the area,” Wamboka said.
He termed the incident an act of political intolerance, insisting that the movement would not be intimidated or silenced by the destruction of its property.
“This cowardly act of political intolerance and intimidation will not shake our resolve or silence the people’s voice,” he added.
Wamboka further announced that leaders associated with Linda Mwananchi would travel to Matungu as a team to stand with their supporters despite the incident.
“We shall visit Matungu as a team, stand with our supporters and reaffirm our commitment to the people-driven movement,” he said.
The vandalism comes as Ruto continues an eight-day tour of Western Kenya, which has included engagements in Busia, Bungoma and Kakamega counties.
According to the published presidential itinerary, the Head of State is scheduled to visit Matungu on Saturday, November 21, where he is expected to lay the foundation stone for Kenya Medical Training College hostels and launch the Matungu-River Sio Road project.
The President’s visit is part of his wider development and political engagements in the Western region.
Wamboka maintained that the incident would not weaken the movement’s presence in the area, declaring that attacks on its offices would not erase the political aspirations of its supporters.
“You can deface our offices, but you cannot deface the people’s resolve for change. Linda Mwananchi! Linda Kenya!” he said.

items.title: Australia complete record T20I chase at MCG to edge England in thriller
items.summary:
Australia beat England in first T20I as MCG record run-chase earns hosts 1-0 lead in five-match series
Harry Brook hits 68 off 25 balls after being dropped twice, as Australia put down six chances in the field; England add only 68 from final 10 overs, as hosts chase 188 with a ball to spare; second
items.text:
Australia beat England in first T20I as MCG record run-chase earns hosts 1-0 lead in five-match series
Harry Brook hits 68 off 25 balls after being dropped twice, as Australia put down six chances in the field; England add only 68 from final 10 overs, as hosts chase 188 with a ball to spare; second T20I takes place in Carrara on Tuesday (play starts 8.15am UK time)
Saturday 21 November 2026 12:06, UK
Australia pulled off a record T20I run chase of 188 at the MCG to beat England by three wickets with a ball to spare in a thrilling series opener in Melbourne on Saturday.
England captain Harry Brook had tonked 68 off just 25 balls - hitting six sixes - as England posted 187-9, though his side wasted a dominant position of 119-4 at the halfway point of their innings by adding only 68 from the last 10 overs.
Nikhil Chaudhary, who had helped drag Australia back into the contest with the ball - the hosts having dropped six chances - then top-scored with a magnificent 68 off 38 with the bat.
He was dismissed with 20 still required off the final two overs, Australia seven down, but Jack Edwards (25no off 11) struck a couple of crucial sixes in a clutch cameo before finishing the job with a boundary.
After being inserted by the hosts, England's innings had got off to the worst possible start as Phil Salt picked out mid-off first ball, while Aneurin Donald (10) - put down two deliveries prior - perished soon after.
But Brook, dropped on 2 and 3, made Australia pay for their profligacy as he smoked three sixes in a row in taking Riley Meredith's fourth over for 24, the touring captain romping to a 20-ball fifty.
He and Tom Banton (39 off 22) - shelled twice, taking Australia's tally to five inside seven overs - put on 107 for the third wicket, with Adam Zampa also taking some tap as his opening over went for 20.
Both were gone in the space of six deliveries though, Chaudhary's wrist spin accounting for Brook, caught behind, and Banton gone to a sensational diving catch in the deep by debutant Lachlan Shaw.
England stumbled their way to a rather underwhelming score thereafter, despite the best efforts of Jordan Cox (27 off 20) and Sam Curran (21 off 20), the visitors falling short of the 200-run target they'll have surely been eyeing.
That said, it was still a record T20I chase at the MCG for Australia to reel in, and their assignment was made all the tougher when Liam Dawson (1-30) struck in the opening over - Jake Fraser-McGurk (1) bowled when charging the left-arm spinner, deceived in the flight.
Mitch Marsh hammered Henry Crocombe's first ball in T20 international cricket for six over deep backward square for quite the introduction, but the young quick responded well to remove fellow debutant Sam Harper (32 off 15) for his first wicket in his second over.
Harper had provided some impetus to the Australian innings, Jamie Overton's opening over plundered for 21 runs, and Chaudhary maintained that momentum, with useful support from his captain Marsh (37 off 32) and Tim David (20 off 13).
David failed to cash in a huge slice of luck when the bails failed to dislodge as he inside-edged one back onto his stumps, as he departed a ball later to the returning Adil Rashid (1-30).
It prompted a rather sizeable Australian wobble, with three wickets tumbling for 13 runs in little more than an over, and when Chaudhary finally fell - caught in the deep - it looked like England might be in the ascendency, only for Edwards to have other ideas.
In other worrying news for England, Will Jacks left the field late on, splitting the webbing on his hand as Ben Dwarshuis drilled a ball back at him in the penultimate over. He is due to captain the team in the fifth and final T20I of the series as Brook departs for the Test tour of South Africa.
Chaudhary enjoyed 'chirp' with England
Player of the Match, Nikhil Chaudhary:
"I was just trying to hit the wickets at the start and got the big wicket of Harry [Brook]. I wanted to bowl that five, six-metre length. That was my goal.
"With the bat, you knew it was going to be a big game and that there was going to some chirp. I just had to stay stable and play my game.
"Hopefully I did that and won the game for the team, which was great. There is nothing better than playing at the MCG and winning."
Brook: England were 10 runs short
England captain Harry Brook:
"It was a very entertaining game, going down to the last couple of balls. It's what the fans want to see and everybody watching at home.
"We were probably 10 runs short of what we needed on that surface. If we get those, we probably end up winning the game."
'I was worried when we dropped Brook twice!'
Australia captain Mitch Marsh:
"I was worried when we dropped the best batter in the world [Brook] a couple of times. Most of the time you don't deserve to win.
"But outside a few tough chances, I thought the energy and speed was great to watch. They are all good kids.
"It has been a pretty crazy 12 days but right there is the future of the Australian cricket side with all these young guys. Hopefully we can get back to enjoying that.
"They are a great bunch. I want them to not care about making mistakes and enjoy the environment. Hopefully a win like that shows them they belong."
Results/schedule for England's Australia tour
All T20 internationals to start at 8.15am UK time
- First ODI: Australia won by seven wickets in Perth
- Second ODI: England won by 135 runs in Adelaide
- Third ODI: England won by 97 runs in Hobart
- First T20I: Australia won by three wickets in Melbourne
- Second T20I: Tuesday November 24 (Carrara)
- Third T20I: Friday November 27 (Brisbane)
- Fourth T20I: Sunday November 29 (Sydney)
- Fifth T20I: Wednesday December 2 (Canberra)

items.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
items.summary:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The
items.text:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published22 hours ago
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published22 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published22 hours ago
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".
He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take £500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".
He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.
She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

items.title: Sandpapergate: Cummins has Australia’s ‘unanimous support’ as Test captain
items.summary:
Sandpapergate: Cummins has Australia’s ‘unanimous support’ as Test captain
Pat Cummins to remain Test captain after Cricket Australia back cricketer following cheating scandal in South Africa.
Cricket Australia (CA) threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain Test captain on Saturday,
items.text:
Sandpapergate: Cummins has Australia’s ‘unanimous support’ as Test captain
Pat Cummins to remain Test captain after Cricket Australia back cricketer following cheating scandal in South Africa.
Cricket Australia (CA) threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain Test captain on Saturday, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering “Sandpapergate” scandal.
Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.
At a news conference last week, he strenuously denied being aware of what was going on, but his position was undermined when Cameron Bancroft backed Khawaja’s version of events.
Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.
With speculation over Cummins’ future rampant and a home four-Test series against New Zealand next month, CA moved to stamp out any further discussion about the 33-year-old’s fate after meeting him to check on his welfare.
It came after Josh Hazlewood earlier Saturday suggested he could quit if any action was taken against his longtime bowling partner.
CA expressed “its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain” following a board meeting.
“We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn,” said Chairman David Boon.
“We’ve expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.
“We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat’s integrity has been compromised.”
The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner.
After Cummins’ denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a newspaper column by also claiming “it was the whole team” while saying he felt “angry and betrayed” by the Test skipper.
Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening its investigation but instead set up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018.
Hazlewood backs Cummins and denies Sandpapergate knowledge
Cummins said being captain “carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly.
“David and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018,” he added.
“I support the forum 100 percent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say.
“There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth (at the first Test) will be my focus and priority.”
Hazlewood threw his support behind Cummins earlier Saturday and made a veiled threat to call it a day if he was removed as captain.
He reiterated that the bowling group at the time, which also included Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, were not part of the plan.
They jointly released a statement in 2021 denying any involvement.
“I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood told the Sydney Daily Telegraph in his first comments since the story blew up.
“He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.”
Asked if he would consider quitting in protest if Cummins was removed, Hazlewood said: “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah.”
Starc has also reinforced that he knew nothing in recent days. Lyon and Smith have yet to comment.

items.title: Muhoozi cancels $3bn Turkish SGR contract linking Uganda to Kenya
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba has announced the cancellation of a multi-billion-dollar contract awarded to Turkish construction firm Yapi Merkezi to build the country’s Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), throwing the future of the regional infrastruc
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces General Muhoozi Kainerugaba has announced the cancellation of a multi-billion-dollar contract awarded to Turkish construction firm Yapi Merkezi to build the country’s Standard Gauge Railway (SGR), throwing the future of the regional infrastructure project into uncertainty.
Muhoozi, the son of President Yoweri Museveni, said Uganda would seek another contractor to undertake the railway project, which is expected to connect Kampala to Malaba on the Kenyan border.
In a series of posts on X , the military chief declared that the government had terminated the agreement with the Turkish company, without providing details of the circumstances behind the decision.
“We have cancelled the contract with the Turkish company to build the SGR. We will get another one that is more worthy of our country!” he wrote.
He also called on supporters of the Patriotic League of Uganda (PLU), a political organisation he chairs, to organise demonstrations outside the Turkish Embassy in Kampala on June 19.
Muhoozi directed security agencies to allow the protests, saying ordinary Ugandans and his supporters should be permitted to demonstrate at the diplomatic mission.
“PLU should demonstrate on Friday comrade! All Security Services are instructed to leave our supporters/ordinary Ugandans to demonstrate at the Turkish Embassy on Friday 19th June 2026!” he added.
The announcement came amid escalating tensions between Muhoozi and Turkey, with the Ugandan general also demanding that Ankara hand over or expel Ugandan activist and government critic Fred Lumbuye, who has been living in Turkey.
He subsequently suspended the planned demonstration, saying he wanted to visit Greece before making a final decision on Turkey.
The cancellation announcement raised questions about the future of the €2.7 billion (approximately $3 billion) railway contract, which was signed in October 2024 between the Ugandan government and Yapi Merkezi.
The 272-kilometre electric railway is designed to link Kampala with Malaba, where it will connect to Kenya’s existing SGR network, providing landlocked Uganda with a rail connection to the Port of Mombasa.
Contract reversal after Museveni’s intervention
However, Muhoozi’s announcement did not immediately translate into a formally confirmed termination of the contract, with Uganda’s Ministry of Works and Transport yet to publicly clarify the legal status of the agreement.
The military chief later reversed his position on November 6, announcing that Yapi Merkezi had been approved to proceed with the first phase of the railway following instructions from his father, President Museveni.
“Under the direction and instructions of Mzee Museveni, I approve the Turkish company Yapi Merkezi to implement the 1st Phase of the SGR. From Malaba to Kampala,” Muhoozi posted on X.
He further instructed government departments to expedite implementation of the directive.
The latest development has effectively restored the Turkish contractor’s position after months of uncertainty surrounding the project.
A project plagued by delays
Uganda awarded Yapi Merkezi the contract in October 2024 after abandoning an earlier arrangement with China’s China Harbour Engineering Company, which failed to secure the financing required to implement the railway.
President Museveni officially launched construction of the Malaba-Kampala section in November 2024, with the project expected to take four years once major construction works commence.
The railway is part of Uganda’s wider plan to develop a modern rail network linking the country to neighbouring Kenya, South Sudan, Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Its completion is expected to reduce the cost of transporting goods, ease pressure on road networks and strengthen regional trade through the Northern Corridor.
On November 18, Uganda’s government reported that it had paid Shs373 billion in compensation to 7,721 people affected by the railway project, while land acquisition and preparations for construction continued.
The government is targeting January 2027 to achieve financial closure for the $2.97 billion project before authorising full construction works.
The railway’s future has therefore remained tied to financing arrangements, land acquisition and the government’s commitment to the Turkish contractor.

items.title: Free medical camp treats 1,310 residents in Keringet as Mau Forest conservation programme links health to livelihoods
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – A free comprehensive medical camp organised under the Mau Forest Complex conservation programme has treated 1,310 residents in Keringet, Kuresoi South, Nakuru County, as the initiative seeks to link community wellbeing with forest restoration.
Principal Secretary for Environm
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 21 – A free comprehensive medical camp organised under the Mau Forest Complex conservation programme has treated 1,310 residents in Keringet, Kuresoi South, Nakuru County, as the initiative seeks to link community wellbeing with forest restoration.
Principal Secretary for Environment Dr Festus Ng’eno, who is patron of MFC-ICLIP, said the medical camps were part of President William Ruto’s plan to restore the Mau Forest Complex while improving the livelihoods of communities living around the forest.
“This is the plan which His Excellency President William Ruto set for us, to come and facilitate the restoration of the Mau Forest Complex,” he said.
Ng’eno said the programme had committed itself to ensuring communities living within the forest complex were better placed to participate in conservation efforts.
“We committed ourselves to not only restore the Mau but also ensure people living in the Forest Complex are in a better position to participate in conservation. That’s why we brought the medical camps,” he said.
The camp, held at Keringet Boarding Comprehensive School, was the programme’s second medical outreach following an inaugural camp in Kiptagich, which served 3,678 residents with the support of 100 volunteer professionals from various sectors.
The medical camps offer more than 13 services, including consultations, screening, treatment, health education, specialised medical interventions, referrals for patients requiring further care and registration under the Social Health Authority.
The programme says integrating healthcare into its conservation agenda recognises the relationship between community wellbeing, livelihoods and environmental protection.
The Keringet camp was organised in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and several institutions, including Mathari National Teaching and Referral Hospital, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital, Zuri Health, Lions SightFirst Eye Hospital, the National Syndemic Diseases Control Council, the County Government of Nakuru, Kenya Medical Training College and Community Health Promoters.
Biovax and BB Bread also supported the initiative, alongside National Government Administration Officers, volunteers and members of the local community.
The programme says the medical camps are part of efforts to ensure communities living around the Mau Forest Complex benefit from initiatives aimed at restoring the forest while improving their health and livelihoods.

items.title: Iran’s IRGC downs US drone over Hormuz as efforts to end war remain stalled
items.summary:
Iran’s IRGC downs US drone over Hormuz as efforts to end war remain stalled
Iranian foreign minister reiterates conditions for reopening of Strait of Hormuz, as US slaps sanctions on four Iranians it says acted as ‘oil trustees’.
Iranian forces say they have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait
items.text:
Iran’s IRGC downs US drone over Hormuz as efforts to end war remain stalled
Iranian foreign minister reiterates conditions for reopening of Strait of Hormuz, as US slaps sanctions on four Iranians it says acted as ‘oil trustees’.
Iranian forces say they have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz, as the United States steps up its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday a new air defence system had intercepted and shot down the drone, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB. It said the incident marked the 58th US MQ-9 drone brought down by Iranian forces.
The incident comes days after the US and Iran engaged in direct, tit-for-tat strikes, against a backdrop of increasing Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed in peacetime.
Launched by the US and Israel on February 28, the war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted shipping, pushing global energy prices higher and spreading to countries across the region.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but it was never fully implemented because of disagreements over freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with attacks resuming periodically since July. In August, The Washington Post reported that the US had lost 45 MQ-9 drones, or about 25 percent of its fleet at a cost of more than $1.3bn, during combat operations in Iran.
‘No war, no peace’
As an agreement to end the war remains elusive, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday outlined his country’s positions on negotiations with the US, citing a seven-day proposal delivered to the US in September.
In an interview with state media, Araghchi said the seven conditions Iran has put forward “must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen”. The conditions include ending the war and lifting sanctions and the naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports.
Araghchi said Iran was prepared to negotiate how the conditions should be implemented, saying its timetable was “flexible”. The negotiations would be “conditional on the American side taking necessary confidence-building measures”, he added.
The top diplomat also ruled out Iran transferring its stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium abroad, but said a “fair solution” could be reached and a number of proposals by mediators were “worth examining”.
Araghchi said that the current “no war, no peace” state of the conflict was undesirable, but that Iran could not accept an agreement that would “hand victory to the other side”.
At a Friday news conference at the White House, US President Donald Trump told reporters that Tehran “want to make a deal” but not one that is acceptable to him.
“We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years,” alleged Trump, who had said last week that a deal with Iran on ending the war was unnecessary.
At the same news conference, US Vice President JD Vance, who had previously blamed the war for Republicans losing both chambers of Congress earlier this month, declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon.
Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States.”
Separately on Friday, the US Treasury said it had imposed sanctions on four Iranians it said acted as “oil trustees”, collecting money from illicit international oil sales for Iran to evade sanctions and the US naval blockade on its southern ports.
The Treasury said in a statement that in many cases the trustees have kept oil revenues for personal gain. Among the individuals sanctioned are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the Iranian Football Federation’s President Mehdi Taj, the Treasury said.
The new sanctions put the individuals on the Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, freezing any assets they may have under US jurisdiction and effectively prohibiting dollar transactions with them or entities that they control.
The Treasury also said it imposed sanctions on Mohammad Hossein Servati, the son of IRGC Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, who has held positions in companies that brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil for delivery to independent Chinese “teapot” refineries.
Another sanctioned individual is Mojtaba Arabnejad, the son of the sanctioned Mahan Air CEO Hamid Arabnejad. The Treasury said that Mojtaba Arabnejad has purchased aircraft parts for the sanctioned Mahan Air and overseen oil sales that have partly supported the airline.
Defunding offensive activity
Meanwhile, as Republicans grapple with the fallout from the sweeping midterm election losses, Democratic Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Congress to use an upcoming government funding bill to end spending for offensive military operations against Iran.
Citing the mounting costs of the war, they issued a video statement urging fellow legislators to reject any funding package that keeps paying for the war, with a deadline looming next month to adopt a budget.
Failing to pass a spending bill by December 11 could trigger a government shutdown, a risk that has made some Democrats wary of drawing a red line on the war on Iran.
Rosa DeLauro and Patty Murray, the top Democrats responsible for appropriations, have said they would prefer to find ways to end the war without risking a government shutdown.

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 21 – Embakasi East MP Babu Owino has claimed he contributed 99.9 per cent to Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s political growth, insisting their relationship remains intact despite disagreements over the leadership of the Linda Mwananchi political outfit.
